views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Keep the July 6 List 1 tariffs in place and let the List 2 / List 3 comment-and-hearing process run, but do not implement the proposed $200B/10% list early and do not roll anything back. Reopen a structured channel with Beijing aimed at enforceable IP, tech-transfer, and market-access commitments rather than another purchase-only communiqué. Use the still-unused List 3 threat, plus farm-aid time already bought, as bargaining leverage instead of firing the next round into consumer goods while no talks are even scheduled.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is modestly positive, not high. USTR’s March 22 Section 301 findings and Lighthizer’s July characterization of China’s IP/tech-transfer practices as an “existential threat to America’s most critical comparative advantage” identify a real structural injury, and China has now matched List 1 dollar-for-dollar (July 6) while targeting soybeans, autos, and other politically sensitive U.S. exports. Soy is a ~$14B China market; futures fell toward decade lows, farm groups are lobbying against escalation, and USDA on July 24 authorized up to $12B in short-term relief—clear evidence that a key export sector and a core political constituency are already paying. That is the + side of the score. It is not +0.5 or higher because the U.S. macro is not yet bitten: industrial production is still rising, VIX closed 12.29 on July 25, consumer sentiment is only slightly off, and NYT/S&P commentary as of July 24 still judged economy-wide damage scarce. Imports from China actually surged into July (front-loading), and the dollar and a ~7% CNY depreciation (DEXCHUS 6.33 to 6.77) are absorbing some of the tariff hit. The May 19 joint statement showed Beijing will offer purchase volume to get a pause without structural IP change; the White House correctly collapsed that truce on May 29. Further unilateral escalation now—especially List 3 consumer goods (TVs, clothing, ACs)—would raise U.S. costs, invite non-tariff harassment of the large stock of U.S. affiliates in China (China cannot match another $200B in goods tariffs), and spend leverage before any new talks exist. ZTE’s July 13 lift already spent a major non-tariff chip. Hold the existing $34B (and the pending $16B process), keep List 3 as a timed threat through the August hearings, and negotiate for structural terms the May deal never delivered.
key_factors: Section 301 IP/tech-transfer findings remain unremedied after the collapsed May 19 purchase-only truce
List 1 ($34B) and matching Chinese retaliation are already live; List 3 ($200B) is proposed but not in force
U.S. farm-belt exposure is material (soy ~$14B; prices down; $12B USDA aid on July 24)
U.S. macro still resilient (IP up, VIX ~12, no clear GDP hit); China FX depreciation is offsetting some tariff pressure
China cannot match further goods tariffs dollar-for-dollar and may shift to non-tariff pressure on U.S. firms
No public talks scheduled; implementing List 3 now would spend leverage and hit U.S. consumer goods

sources_cited.excerpt: USTR releases Section 301 report finding China's IP/tech-transfer practices unreasonable or discriminatory. Trump signs presidential memorandum directing tariffs on Chinese imports, a WTO case, and investment restrictions.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
List 1 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$34B of Chinese goods. China imposes matching ~$34B retaliation the same day.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines). Public comment / hearing process begins.
U.S. imports from China rose to $47.0B in July 2018 from $39.0B in February, consistent with front-loading ahead of tariffs.
VIX closed 12.29 on 2018-07-25; equity vol not signaling a macro crisis.
CNY weakened from 6.33 in late January to 6.77 on 2018-07-25 (~6.8%), offsetting part of the U.S. tariff wedge.
U.S. industrial production index 103.36 in July 2018, still rising over the window.
USDA authorized up to $12B in programs, in line with an estimated $11B impact of retaliatory tariffs on U.S. agricultural goods.
Nearly one-third of U.S. soybeans, or about $14 billion, is sent to China each year; China’s 25% tariff targets that flow.

Lighthizer: China’s IP practices are an existential threat to America’s most critical comparative advantage. No plans for additional meetings have been made public. List 3 hits consumer products; hearings start in August.
Commerce lifted the ZTE denial order after a $1B penalty, $400M escrow, management overhaul, and 10-year compliance monitors.
As of mid-July, evidence that the trade war is doing meaningful economy-wide damage is scarce; direct effects are small because the U.S. economy is mostly domestically driven.
